items.prompt: How many index subsets exist for n distinct indexed elements?

feedback.reason: Every one of n positions contributes a binary membership choice.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

For each indexed element, a subset makes one of two independent decisions: exclude it or include it. Multiplying two choices across n positions gives 2 · 2 · ... · 2 = 2^n. This counts index subsets, including the empty and full subsets; it does not arrange selected elements, so neither n! nor an order-based count applies.

items: With n = 3, the eight decisions are 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110 and 111.
Bit i records the decision for indexed element i; the element's value does not affect the count.
The count changes only when the result contract identifies equal-valued occurrences as the same output.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Use 2^n only for independent include/exclude decisions over n indexed positions. Permutations answer a different question because they distinguish order.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_factorial: A factorial counts complete orderings; subsets preserve no choice order and may contain fewer than n elements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_squared: A quadratic count describes pairs of positions, not all independent include/exclude combinations.

items.prompt: Which mask range enumerates every subset of n indexed elements exactly once?

feedback.reason: Every n-bit pattern is one subset encoding.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

There are exactly 2^n n-bit patterns, and the integers in the half-open interval [0, 2^n) are exactly those patterns. The lower boundary 0 is 00...0 and encodes the empty subset. The last included value, 2^n - 1, is 11...1 and encodes the full subset. The value 2^n itself needs bit n, so it lies outside the n-position mapping.

items: Start at 0 so the empty subset is not lost.
Stop before 2^n because it is the first value that needs n + 1 bits.
Incrementing by one visits each integer, and therefore each n-bit pattern, once.

blocks.title: Boundary case
blocks.text: The boundary masks are a useful proof: 0 selects none, while 2^n - 1 has all n low bits set. Use the half-open range [0, 2^n) so neither is missed or repeated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_to_two_n: Starting at one omits the empty subset, while 2^n sets bit n outside the declared positions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_to_n_minus_one: This visits only n masks even though n binary positions encode 2^n distinct membership patterns.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_to_n_factorial: The factorial boundary counts orderings and also includes many values that are not n-bit subset masks.

items.prompt: What subset does mask 0 represent?

feedback.reason: No set bit selects any indexed element.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Membership of element i is read from bit i. In mask 0, every bit is zero, so every membership test returns false and no element is appended. The result is therefore the empty subset. This is not an invalid special case: the empty subset belongs to every power set, including the power set of an empty input.

items: For each i, evaluate mask AND (1 shifted left by i).
Every result is zero because mask itself contains no one bits.
Append nothing and return the initialized empty subset.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Read the mask from bit 0 upward and translate each 1 through the index mapping. This prevents treating the printed binary string as a list of values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_only: Selecting the first element requires bit 0 to be one, which would make the mask value at least one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.full: The full subset requires all n mapped bits to be one; zero has none of those bits set.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.invalid: The empty subset is required by the power-set definition and is represented canonically by the all-zero mask.

items.prompt: What mask represents the full subset of n elements when bits 0 through n - 1 map to those elements?

feedback.reason: The full subset needs every one of the n low positions set.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The full subset requires bits 0 through n - 1 to be one. The value 1 shifted left by n is the pattern 1 followed by n zeros. Subtracting one borrows through those zeros and produces n low ones: for n = 4, 10000 - 1 = 01111. Thus (1 shifted left by n) - 1 selects exactly every mapped position.

items: First create the exclusive boundary 2^n with a one at position n.
Subtract one to turn positions 0 through n - 1 into ones.
Confirm that no position outside the n-element mapping remains set.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_shift_n: This selects only bit n, which is just outside the mapped positions 0 through n - 1.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Zero clears every mapped membership bit and therefore represents the empty subset, not the full one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n: The numeric value n does not generally contain n low one bits; for example, four is binary 0100.

items.prompt: If bit position i maps to elements[i], when is that element included in the subset encoded by mask?

options.text: When mask AND (1 shifted left by i) is nonzero.
When that AND result is zero.
Only when mask numerically equals i.

feedback.reason: Subset decoding is a membership test at each mapped position.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The probe 1 shifted left by i has exactly one set bit, at position i. AND keeps that bit only when mask also has bit i set. A nonzero result therefore proves membership of elements[i]; zero proves exclusion. Comparing the whole mask with i confuses a set encoding with an index, and the parity of i has no role in the mapping.

items: Build the one-bit probe 1 shifted left by i.
Intersect the probe with mask using bitwise AND.
Append elements[i] exactly when the intersection is nonzero.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.i_even: Even and odd indices use the same membership rule; only the bit at position i matters.

items.prompt: For elements [A, B, C, D], which subset is encoded by mask 1010 when bit 0 maps to A?

feedback.reason: The set bits are positions 1 and 3; with bit 0 mapped to A, they select B and D.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Binary digits are conventionally written with the most significant bit on the left. In 1010, the one bits are therefore at positions 3 and 1, counted from the right starting at zero. The declared mapping is 0→A, 1→B, 2→C and 3→D, so those positions select B and D. Reading the printed characters left-to-right as A through D reverses the mapping.

items: Annotate 1010 as positions 3, 2, 1, 0 from left to right.
Keep positions whose digit is one: positions 3 and 1.
Translate through the index mapping to obtain D and B, or {B, D} in input order.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Read the mask from bit 0 upward and translate each 1 through the index mapping. This prevents treating the printed binary string as a list of values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a_b_c: This answer requires positions 0, 1 and 2, but the given mask sets only positions 1 and 3.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c_d: Selecting C and D requires positions 2 and 3; here position 2 is zero while position 1 is one.

items.prompt: The input values are [X, X] at two distinct indices. How many index subsets do two bits encode?

options.text: Four index subsets, though some materialized value lists may be equal.
Three subsets because equal values merge automatically.
One subset because both values are equal.

feedback.reason: Bitmask enumeration naturally enumerates subsets of indexed occurrences.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The two X values occupy different indices, so the mask assigns them different bits. The four masks are 00→[], 01→[X at index 0], 10→[X at index 1], and 11→[both occurrences]. The two singleton masks materialize the same value list [X], but they remain distinct index subsets. A value-distinct result contract would need an explicit deduplication rule.

items: Count occurrences by position before considering whether their values are equal.
Enumerate 2^2 masks because there are two independent positional choices.
Only merge equal materialized outputs if the problem explicitly asks for value-distinct subsets.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two: Two counts individual positions, not all combinations of excluding or including each of those positions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one: Equal values do not erase the identity of their input positions under an index-subset contract.

items.prompt: Does increasing numeric mask order enumerate subsets by increasing subset size?

options.text: No. Numeric order follows binary value, not popcount.
Yes. Every later mask contains more set bits.
Only when input values are sorted.

feedback.reason: Numeric mask order changes membership according to binary counting.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Numeric order performs ordinary binary counting, including carries. A carry can clear several one bits before setting a higher bit, so popcount can decrease: 0011 has two selected positions, while its successor 0100 has one. To enumerate by subset size, group or generate masks by popcount instead of assuming numeric order provides that property.

items: Numeric order guarantees complete, unique coverage of masks.
Popcount determines subset size independently of numeric value.
A required cardinality order needs an additional ordering strategy.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Read the mask from bit 0 upward and translate each 1 through the index mapping. This prevents treating the printed binary string as a list of values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_always: The transition 0011→0100 decreases popcount from two to one, so later masks need not contain larger subsets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_even_n: The carry behavior that changes popcount occurs for any sufficient width and is unrelated to whether n is even.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_sorted_values: Numeric mask order depends solely on bit patterns; sorting element values cannot make it a popcount order.

items.prompt: Why must the representation provide at least n usable mask bits to encode subsets of n indexed elements in one word?

options.text: Each element needs its own independent membership position.
The largest element value determines width.
Each sorted rank needs two bits.
Only the empty subset requires n bits.

feedback.reason: A one-word subset mask allocates one boolean slot per element index.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The encoding must distinguish membership of every index independently, so index i needs its own bit i. A word with w usable bits can therefore encode this mapping only when n ≤ w. If n exceeds w, a shift may overflow, wrap, or discard a required position depending on the language; use a wider integer, arbitrary-precision value, bitset, or multiple words instead.

items: Width follows the number of indexed membership decisions, not the magnitude of element values.
The highest required position is n - 1, so positions 0 through n - 1 must all be usable.
Check the language's signedness and shift rules before constructing 1 shifted left by n.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Read the mask from bit 0 upward and translate each 1 through the index mapping. This prevents treating the printed binary string as a list of values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_value: Element magnitudes are stored elsewhere; the mask width depends on how many independent index memberships it must record.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_order: Sorting can change which index maps to a position, but each position still needs only one boolean membership bit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.empty_subset: The same n-position representation must also encode every nonempty subset, including the full all-ones mask.

items.prompt: Which statements about n-bit subset masks are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bit i records membership of indexed element i.
Numeric mask order is the same as nondecreasing subset-size order.

feedback.reason: Subset masks are positional membership encodings.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Under the declared positional contract, bit i directly records membership of indexed element i. The two boundary patterns then follow: all zeros selects none, while the n low ones in 2^n - 1 select all n positions. Numeric order is a different property: binary carries can reduce popcount, as in 0011→0100, so it does not sort subsets by cardinality.

items: Accept `zero_empty`: no set position means no selected element.
Accept `full_all_ones`: 2^n - 1 contains ones at every mapped position.
Accept `bit_membership`: this is the defining index-to-bit invariant.
Reject `numeric_order_size`: numeric value and number of set bits are not monotonically coupled.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Check claims against the positional contract. Numeric mask order is binary counting; it is not automatically an order by subset size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_order_size: Binary counting can clear several low ones during a carry, so consecutive numeric masks can decrease in subset size.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.full_all_ones: All n low bits are set.

items.prompt: Which tests are important for subset-mask enumeration? Select all that apply.

options.text: n = 0, which should yield one empty subset.
n = 1, which should yield empty and singleton subsets.

feedback.reason: The empty-domain identity and both mask extremes expose off-by-one errors.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

For n = 0, the range [0, 1) must run once and decode mask 0 as the empty subset; code that returns nothing has mishandled the power-set identity. For n = 1, masks 0 and 1 test both exclusion and inclusion. The final all-ones mask proves the upper bound is inclusive in effect. One middle mask exercises neither boundary and cannot expose an omitted empty or full subset.

items: Accept `n_zero` to test the one-empty-subset identity.
Accept `n_one` to test both values of a single membership bit.
Accept `full_mask` to catch a loop that stops one mask too early.
Reject `only_middle` because it cannot establish correct boundary coverage.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Check claims against the positional contract. Numeric mask order is binary counting; it is not automatically an order by subset size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_middle: A middle mask may decode correctly even when the loop omits mask 0 or stops before the final all-ones mask.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.n_zero: The power set of the empty set contains the empty set.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.full_mask: It verifies inclusion of every element.

items.prompt: Which tasks are performed when materializing one subset from a mask? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the relevant n bit positions.
Test whether each mapped bit is set.
Append selected elements to the output subset.
Sort bit positions before every membership test.

feedback.reason: Decoding maps positional membership into a concrete subset.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Materialization starts with an empty result and examines the n mapped positions. At each i, the decoder tests mask AND (1 shifted left by i) and appends elements[i] only for a nonzero result. Iterating i in input order already yields an index-ordered subset. Sorting bit positions would add work without changing their fixed numeric order or the membership decision.

items: Accept `inspect_positions`: every mapped membership may affect the result.
Accept `test_membership`: the current bit decides whether the element belongs.
Accept `append_selected`: materialization must copy selected values into the result.
Reject `sort_mask_bits`: positions already have the stable order 0 through n - 1.

blocks.text: Check claims against the positional contract. Numeric mask order is binary counting; it is not automatically an order by subset size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_mask_bits: Bit positions are already numbered in a fixed order, so sorting before each test is redundant and adds unnecessary cost.

items.prompt: Which statements distinguish index subsets from value-distinct subsets? Select all that apply.

options.text: Equal-valued input positions still correspond to different mask bits.
Different masks can materialize equal value sequences when input values repeat.
Producing only value-distinct subsets requires an additional duplicate-control contract.
Equal values automatically share one mask bit.

feedback.reason: Bitmask enumeration is exact for indexed power sets.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Plain masks encode occurrence identity: equal values at indices i and j still receive separate bits and may be selected independently. Consequently, two different masks can materialize the same sequence of values. If the required output identifies such sequences as one result, the algorithm needs a separate value-level duplicate policy; changing the positional meaning of the mask would alter which occurrence choices are representable.

items: Accept `indices_independent`: mask bits belong to positions, not value classes.
Accept `duplicate_outputs`: different positional choices may render equal values.
Accept `needs_dedup_contract`: uniqueness must be defined and enforced separately.
Reject `masks_merge_equal`: a plain mask has no knowledge of value equality.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A mask distinguishes occurrences by index, even when their values are equal. If the output requires value-distinct subsets, deduplication is an additional rule, not a property of the mask.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.masks_merge_equal: Plain bitmasks map one bit to each indexed occurrence and do not automatically merge positions that store equal values.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_outputs: Value equality can collapse distinct index choices.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.needs_dedup_contract: Plain masks do not infer it.

items.prompt: Arrange the outer algorithm for enumerating every subset mask.

elements.text: Decode the current mask into its subset.
Increment mask and repeat while mask is below the limit.

feedback.reason: The half-open mask range [0, 2^n) includes every n-bit pattern exactly once.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The loop needs an exclusive upper bound before it can establish its valid mask domain. It then starts at zero so the empty subset is included. Decoding must happen before incrementing, otherwise mask 0 is skipped. Repeating while mask is below 2^n processes the final valid pattern 2^n - 1 and stops before the first value that needs bit n.

items: Compute limit = 2^n after confirming the representation can express that boundary.
Initialize mask = 0.
Decode the current mask under the fixed index-to-bit mapping.
Increment mask and repeat while mask < limit.

blocks.title: Boundary case
blocks.text: Trace n = 2: decode 00, 01, 10 and 11, then stop when mask becomes 100. Any different boundary loses or adds a state.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for decoding one mask into an ordered subset.

elements.text: Iterate element indices from 0 through n - 1.
Append elements[i] when the bit is set.

feedback.reason: The decoding order follows element indices, while membership follows mask bits.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The output container must exist before any selected element can be appended. Iterating indices establishes the stable output order. For the current i, a one-bit probe determines membership; only after that test can the decoder conditionally append elements[i]. These last two operations repeat inside the index loop rather than occurring once after it.

items: Initialize an empty output subset.
Iterate i from 0 through n - 1.
Test whether mask AND (1 shifted left by i) is nonzero.
If it is nonzero, append elements[i]; then continue with the next i.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: Testing before appending is the decision boundary. Appending first and trying to undo a zero bit obscures the invariant and invites stale elements.

items.prompt: Arrange the reasoning for the full-subset mask.

elements.text: Require bits 0 through n - 1 to be one.
Form 1 shifted left by n, with one at position n.
Subtract one to turn the n low positions into ones.
Decode the result to obtain every indexed element.

feedback.reason: The identity 2^n - 1 produces exactly n low one bits.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Start from the representation requirement: the full subset needs ones at positions 0 through n - 1. Shifting one left by n creates the next power of two, whose binary form has one at position n and zeros below it. Subtracting one borrows through those n zeros, leaving exactly the required low ones. Decoding then selects every mapped element.

items: Require one bits at all mapped positions 0 through n - 1.
Form 1 shifted left by n, placing the only one just above those positions.
Subtract one, producing n low one bits.
Decode the resulting mask and confirm that all n indexed elements are selected.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: The derivation assumes that 1 shifted left by n is representable. Check the language and numeric width instead of relying on overflowing fixed-width arithmetic.

items.prompt: Arrange the review process for repeated input values in mask enumeration.

elements.text: State whether subsets are defined by indices or by values.
Recognize that plain masks enumerate index subsets.
Check whether different index masks materialize equal value results.
Keep them or add separate value-level duplicate control according to the contract.

feedback.reason: Duplicate behavior follows the result identity contract.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The result's identity rule comes first because it decides whether equal-valued occurrences are distinct. Plain masks then enumerate index subsets without consulting values. Comparing the materialized results reveals whether different masks collide at the value level. Only then can the implementation preserve both outputs or apply a stated value-level duplicate rule without silently changing the contract.

items: State whether output identity is based on input indices or materialized values.
Recognize that one bit per position enumerates index subsets.
Check whether repeated values make different masks render equal outputs.
Keep those outputs or apply explicit value-level duplicate control according to the stated identity rule.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Do not deduplicate before defining identity. Under an index-subset contract, removing one of two equal singleton occurrences would delete a valid result.

items.prompt: An algorithm iterates every n-bit mask but performs only O(1) work per mask and does not materialize subsets. Select time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: Only the current mask and a constant-size accumulator are stored.

feedback.reason: The exponential factor comes from the number of masks.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The loop visits every integer in [0, 2^n), so it has exactly 2^n iterations. At O(1) work per iteration, total time is 2^n · O(1) = O(2^n). The current mask and constant-size accumulator do not grow with n, and no subsets or history are retained, so auxiliary space is O(1). This conclusion would change if decoding scanned n positions per mask.

items: Count iterations: 2^n masks.
Multiply by the declared O(1) work per mask: O(2^n) time.
Count peak retained state, not cumulative iterations: O(1) auxiliary space.

blocks.title: Cost model
blocks.text: Do not add an n factor merely because masks have n logical bits. The prompt explicitly makes processing one mask O(1); complexity follows performed operations, not the diagram used to describe a state.

items.prompt: An algorithm materializes every subset by scanning all n bit positions for each mask. Select total time and output space.
constraints: Each subset is stored as its selected elements.

feedback.reason: Every mask scans n positions, and the total number of emitted element occurrences across the power set is Θ(n·2^n).

blocks.text: How to reason it out

There are 2^n masks and the decoder checks n positions for each, giving n · 2^n membership tests and O(n·2^n) time. Output space has the same asymptotic bound for a tighter reason: each of the n elements appears in exactly half of all subsets, so the stored element occurrences total n · 2^(n-1) = Θ(n·2^n), in addition to 2^n subset containers.

items: Time: 2^n masks × n tested positions = O(n·2^n).
Stored elements: n positions × 2^(n-1) subsets containing each position = Θ(n·2^n).
The Θ(2^n) subset containers are dominated by the stored-element term when n grows.

blocks.title: Cost model
blocks.text: Separate auxiliary space from output space. A streaming visitor may keep only one O(n) subset, but returning the complete power set requires space proportional to all emitted elements.

items.prompt: A naive algorithm enumerates all 2^n masks, computes popcount(mask) in O(n), and materializes only masks with exactly k set bits. Select worst-case time and output space in terms of C(n,k).
constraints: Each retained subset stores k elements.

feedback.reason: Filtering after full mask enumeration does not remove the cost of inspecting all masks.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The algorithm still visits all 2^n masks. Because the stated popcount costs O(n) for each one, filtering costs 2^n · O(n) = O(n·2^n), even though only C(n,k) masks survive. Exactly C(n,k) subsets are returned and each stores k elements, so output space is O(k·C(n,k)). A direct k-combination generator could avoid the full-mask scan, but that is not the algorithm described.

items: Visited candidates: 2^n, regardless of how many pass the filter.
Work per candidate: O(n) for the declared popcount, yielding O(n·2^n) time.
Retained results: C(n,k) subsets × k stored elements = O(k·C(n,k)) output space.

blocks.title: Cost model
blocks.text: Do not substitute the output count C(n,k) for the number of inspected candidates. That would describe a direct combination generator, not filter-after-enumeration.
